planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; never collect plants from the wild — source only from reputable native plant nurseries with documented propagation.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade, never from wild-collected stock. White fringed orchid is one of the showiest native bog orchids of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, producing a dense spike of pure white flowers in mid to late summer, each bloom trimmed with a delicately fringed lip that gives the species its name, rising above narrow grass-like leaves in open, sunny sphagnum bogs and wet pine savannas. It grows alongside pitcher plants and sundews in the wild and makes a spectacular companion for them in a home bog garden, though like most native orchids it depends on specific soil mycorrhizal fungi and resents root disturbance, so leave established plantings undisturbed once sited. Keep the growing medium constantly wet using rain water or distilled water, since mineral-laden tap water and ordinary fertile soil are both fatal to bog orchids over time.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty soil in partial to full shade; small green wood orchid grows in boggy woods, seepage swamps, and streamhead pocosins across a wide range from Canada to the Gulf Coast, tolerating more shade than most native bog orchids.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into consistently wet, acidic, peaty soil in partial to full shade, never from wild-collected stock. Small green wood orchid is a diminutive, easily overlooked native bog orchid with an unusually wide range from eastern Canada south to the Gulf Coast, distinguished by its small spikes of pale greenish-white flowers with a distinctive club-shaped spur, blooming in mid to late summer in the boggy, shaded woods, seepage swamps, and streamhead pocosins it calls home. Unlike the sun-loving fringed orchids of open savannas, it tolerates and even prefers the dappled shade of a wooded bog margin, making it a useful native orchid for a shaded corner of a bog garden that gets too little sun for showier species. It depends on soil mycorrhizal fungi like other native orchids, so keep the planting undisturbed and consistently wet with rain water or distilled water rather than mineral-rich tap water.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in wet, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; bog yellow-eyed grass grows naturally in the same wet pine savannas, ditches, and bog margins as pitcher plants and sundews across the eastern and Gulf Coastal Plain.

directions: Plant divisions in wet, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; bog yellow-eyed grass forms a low, grass-like tuft of flattened, sword-shaped leaves topped in summer by wiry stalks bearing small, tightly packed brown flower heads that pop open a few tiny bright-yellow, three-petaled flowers at a time each morning. It grows naturally scattered through the same wet, acidic pine savannas, roadside ditches, and bog margins that support pitcher plants, sundews, and orchids across the eastern and Gulf Coastal Plain, and pairs well with those species as an easy, low-key textural companion in a home bog garden. Unlike the true carnivorous plants it shares habitat with, it tolerates a somewhat wider range of soil fertility, but still performs best with constantly wet, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions and full sun. Established clumps slowly increase and self-seed in a favorable bog planting with little additional care.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow standing water or saturated, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; ten-angle pipewort grows naturally in the shallow, nutrient-poor pools and ditches of Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine savannas alongside pitcher plants and grass pink orchids.

directions: Plant divisions in shallow standing water or saturated, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in full sun; ten-angle pipewort produces a low tuft of grass-like leaves and, in summer, tall, wiry, ribbed flower stalks tipped with small, tight, button-like white flower heads that stand well above the foliage like a field of pins stuck upright in the bog, giving rise to the common name hatpins. It grows naturally in the shallow, nutrient-poor pools, ditches, and savanna wetlands of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, often standing in an inch or two of water alongside pitcher plants, grass pink orchids, and sundews, and makes an unusual vertical accent in a home bog garden pool. Keep the crown in consistently saturated to shallowly flooded, acidic, low-fertility soil and full sun, and avoid any fertilizer, which quickly favors weeds over this slow, specialized wetland native.

planting.note: Scatter divisions or seed on the surface of wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade at the edge of a bog planting; zigzag bladderwort is one of the smallest and most easily grown terrestrial bladderworts, self-seeding readily in a wet Gulf Coast bog garden.

directions: Scatter divisions or seed on the surface of wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun to partial shade at the edge of a bog planting. Zigzag bladderwort is a diminutive native carnivorous plant whose thread-like stems and tiny underground bladder traps are almost invisible in the wet sand or peat where it grows, becoming noticeable only when its wiry, zigzagging flower stalks send up small, snapdragon-like yellow flowers a few inches above the substrate from spring through fall. It is one of the easiest bladderworts to establish, self-seeding and spreading quickly through favorable wet, acidic, sunny bog conditions across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, often appearing as a volunteer around sundews and pitcher plants in a home bog garden. Keep the growing medium constantly wet with rain water or distilled water, since it shares the same intolerance of tap water minerals and fertilizer common to all carnivorous plants.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, sandy peat in full sun to partial shade; Carolina redroot spreads by its namesake bright red-orange rhizomes through the same fire-maintained pine savanna wetlands that support pitcher plants along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain.

directions: Plant divisions in wet to saturated, acidic, sandy peat in full sun to partial shade; Carolina redroot forms a fan of woolly, gray-green, sword-shaped leaves and sends up branched flower stalks in summer bearing small, fuzzy, cream-to-yellow flowers with a distinctive woolly texture, but the plant's real signature lies underground, where the thick, spreading rhizomes are a vivid blood-red-orange, historically used by Native peoples and early settlers as a dye and medicinal plant. It grows through the same fire-maintained, nutrient-poor pine savanna wetlands as pitcher plants and orchids along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, spreading steadily by rhizome to form colonies in consistently wet, sunny, acidic ground. In a home bog garden it adds bold vertical foliage contrast to the low rosettes of sundews and butterworts, and divisions establish readily as long as the soil never dries out.
